Formal Language and Automata
UNIT I
FINITE AUTOMATA AND REGULAR EXPRESSION

Agenda of this Session
• Introduction to Automaton

Introduction to Automaton
• The mathematical theory of a simple class of algorithms that are important in computer
sciences and mathematics is called the theory of automata.
• It has primarily two applications in computer science
1. Modeling of Finite State Systems
2. Description of regular sets of finite words
• It has many emerging applications such as
• Computer algorithms and programs
• Verification and specification of protocols
• Designing of compilers
• Searching for patterns in texts
• Natural Language Processing

Introduction to Automaton (Cont..)
• Algorithms are recipes that tell us how to solve problems
• Initially, mathematicians were interested in the dividing line between what was and what
was not algorithmic
• There are two approaches to classify algorithms
1. According to their running times and is known as complexity theory
2. According to the types of memory used in implementing them and is known as
language theory

Automata – What is it?
• The term “Automata” is derived from the Greek Word "αὐτόματα" which
means “self-acting”
• An automaton (Automata in plural) is an abstract self-propelled
computing device which follows a predetermined sequence of operations
automatically
• Automata theory deals with the logic of computation with respect to
simple machines, referred to as automata
• Through automata, computer scientists are able to understand how
machines compute functions and solve problems and more

Automata – What is it? (Cont..)
• Automatons are abstract models of machines that perform computations on an input by
moving through a series of states or configurations
• At each state of the computation, a transition function determines the next
configuration on the basis of a finite portion of the present configuration
• Once the computation reaches an accepting configuration, it accepts that input
• Example : Electric Switch
• Other examples : Fan Regulator, Automatic door controller
BATTERY
Input
: switch
Output
: light bulb
Actions
: flip switch
States
: on, off

Families of Automata
• There are four major families of automaton:
• Finite Automata – Regular Languages
• Pushdown Automata – Context free
• Linear-bounded Automata – Context sensitive
• Turing Machine – Recursively enumerable
• Finite Automata is the simplest automata and Turing Machine is the most complex and the
most powerful automata

– Regular Languages • Pushdown Automata – Context free • Linear-bounded Automata – Context sensitive • Turing Machine – Recursively enumerable • Finite Automata is the simplest automata and Turing Machine is the most complex and the most powerful automata

History of Automata Theory
• This was originated in 1930s, before the existence
of modern computers
• Well-renowned computer scientist Alan Turing
conceived the first “infinite” (or unbounded)
model of computation: the Turing machine in
1936
• Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, two
neurophysiologists, were the first to present a
description of finite automata in 1943
• Later, two computer scientists, G.H.Mealy and
E.F.Moore generalized the theory to much more
powerful machines

Agenda of this Session
• Formal Languages: Strings, Languages, Properties

Alphabet
• An alphabet is a finite set of symbols denoted by ∑
• Examples:
∑= {𝑎, 𝑏}
∑= 0,1 is a binary alphabet
∑= {𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐… 𝑧, 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶… 𝑍} is a character alphabet
∑= {0,1,2, … 9}

String
• A string over some alphabet is a finite sequence of symbols drawn from that alphabet.
Example: ∑= 0,1
Strings = {011, 100, 0101, 111, …….}
• The term sentence and word are often used as synonyms for the term “string”.
• The length of a string s, written as |s| is the no. of occurrences of symbols in s.
• E.g. banana is a special string of length 6.
• The empty string is a special string of length 0.
• The reverse of a string 𝑢is denoted as 𝑢𝑅
Example: u=abab uR=baba

Some common terms associated with parts of a String

Kleene Closure
• The set of all strings including the empty string on the alphabet is written as ∑*
• This is also known as Kleene closure or Kleene star after the famous logician who was one of the
founders of this concept
• For example
∑ = { 1 }, then ∑* = { ε, 1, 11, 111,…..}
∑ = { a, b }, then ∑* = { ε, a, b, ab, ba, aaa, bbb, abab, baba, bbbaa, …..}

Language
• The term language denotes any set of strings over some fixed alphabet.
• Let ∑ be an alphabet and ∑* be the set of all strings on the alphabet ∑. Any subset of ∑* is called
a language over ∑ or language with alphabet ∑
• Generally, language is denoted by L and L ⊆∑*
• Abstract languages like , the empty set or {}, the set containing only empty string are language
under this definition.
Examples:
• All the syntactically well formed pascal programs form a language.
• All grammatically correct English sentences form a language.

Operations on Language
• There are several important operations that can be applied to languages.
• The exponentiation operator to languages can be generalized by defining 𝐿0 to be {} and

Concatenation of a string
• If x and y are strings, then the concatenate of x and y, written xy is the string formed by appending
y to x.
• For example:
x = dog
y = house
xy = doghouse
• The empty string is the identity element under concatenation.

• Finite Automata
• Deterministic Finite Automata

Finite State Automata
• Finite automata is a machine that given an input, jumps through a series of states according to a transition function
• It is a model of behaviour composed of states, transitions and actions
• Finite state machines are widely used in
• Modelling of application behaviour
• Design of hardware digital systems
• Software engineering
• Study of computation and languages

Finite State Automata (Cont..)
• Finite automata is a mathematical model of a system with discrete inputs and outputs
• It consists of a finite set of states and a set of transitions that occur on input symbols chosen from an alphabet set Σ
• One of these states is called the initial state from where the automata begins. There can be one or more final states.
• Examples:
Operation of an elevator
Operation of a switch

Picturization of Finite Automata
• A finite automata can be picturized as a finite control which is in some state from Q, reading a sequence of symbols
from Σ written on a tape as shown below
• In one move, the finite automata does the following:
1. Reads an input symbol
2. Moves its head one position to the right
3. Moves to a state as defined by δ

Deterministic Finite Automata
The finite automata model that allows exactly one transition from a state on an input symbol is called Deterministic Finite
Automata (DFA)
An input string is accepted by a DFA if it reaches one of the final states on reading the input string

Formal Definition of a Finite Automata
A finite automata can be formally denoted by a
five-tuple ( Q, Σ, δ, q0, F )
where
Q → set of states
Σ → input alphabet
δ → transition function : Q X ∑ → Q
q0 → initial state
F → set of final states, , F ⊆Q
Formal definition of this automata is
( { q0, q1, q2, q3 }, { a, b }, δ, q0, {q2} )
where δ is defined as
δ ( q0 , a ) = q1
δ ( q0 , b ) = q3
δ ( q1 , a ) = q1
δ ( q1 , b ) = q2
δ ( q2 , a ) = q1
δ ( q2 , b ) = q2
δ ( q3 , a ) = q3
δ ( q3 , b ) = q3

Acceptance of input strings by DFA
• A string is accepted by a DFA if and only if the DFA
starting at the initial state ends in an accepting state
after reading the string
• The language accepted by a DFA is the set of all
strings accepted by the DFA
Example:
Check whether the string 101101 is accepted by the
DFA given below. Also find the language accepted by
the DFA.
Acceptance of string
δ ( q0 , 101101 ) = δ ( q3 , 01101 )
= δ ( q2 , 1101 )
= δ ( q1 , 101 )
= δ ( q2 , 01 )
= δ ( q3 , 1 )
= q0
On reading the input 101101, the DFA ends in the final
state q0. Hence the input is accepted.

• Non-Deterministic Finite Automata

Non-Deterministic Finite Automata
• The finite automata model that allows 0 or 1 or more transitions from a state on an input symbol is called Non-
Deterministic Finite Automata (NFA)
• As NFA allows more than one transition from a state, at any time, the finite control can be in any number of states.
• When a choice of next state is made, we can imagine that duplicate copies of the automata are made
• An input string will be accepted by a NFA if there is at least one path that ends in a final state
Example:
Design a NFA to accept strings that start with a and end with b over Σ = { a, b }
